intro.html: There are gentle ways and rough ways to get people to do what you want. This topic runs from the softest (a patient, kind word) through sweet talk and temptation to force and threats. Telling them apart helps you judge the characters you read about.

Gentle: coax. Sweet talk: cajole, wheedle. Temptation and charm: entice, lure, beguile. Force: compel (can be neutral), coerce (by threats), browbeat (by bullying), extort (getting money or favors by threats).
Two Latin roots sit inside the forceful ones: pel, drive or push (compel, propel, expel), and tort, twist (extort, contort, torture).

words.ex: Lila {coaxed} the frightened kitten out from under the porch with a little tuna.
words.ctx: The old engine would not start at first, but after twenty minutes of patient tinkering, the mechanic {coaxed} it back to life.

mn.text: The kitten is stuck high in the tree, so Lila holds up a treat and speaks softly, “Come on, sweetie,” until it creeps down: she {coaxes} it.

scene.alt: A girl gently holds up a treat to coax a frightened kitten down from a tree.

words.def: to persuade with flattery or sweet talk
words.ex: Dev {cajoled} his sister into lending him her bike by praising her cooking all week.
words.ctx: When orders failed, the coach tried to {cajole} the team instead, telling them how talented they were and promising pizza if they ran just three more laps.

mn.text: Dev praises his sister’s cooking all week in his jolliest voice until she agrees to lend him her bike: he {cajoles} her.

scene.alt: A teen offers flowers and compliments to his sister, who suspects he wants her bike.

words.def: to get something by flattery or sweet talk
words.ex: The puppy {wheedled} a bite of toast from everyone at the table.
words.ctx: Instead of asking directly, Pip tried to {wheedle} a later bedtime out of his parents, praising their cooking and offering to fold the laundry first.

mn.text: “You’re the best grandpa in the whole world,” Ivy sighs. “Pleeease, may I have another ice cream?” She is trying to {wheedle} one out of him.

scene.alt: A little girl sweet-talks her grandfather for another ice cream, and he melts.

words.def: to attract or tempt by offering something pleasant
words.ex: The smell of popcorn {enticed} us into the theater lobby.
words.ctx: To {entice} new members, the chess club offered free lessons and hot cocoa at every meeting, and soon three times as many students showed up.

mn.cue: en-TICE: ICE cream draws you IN
mn.text: A big sign for cold ice cream hangs over the shop on a hot day, and everyone walking by turns and heads inside: the sign {entices} them.

labels.text: en-TICE: ICE cream pulls you IN

scene.alt: On a hot day, two children are drawn toward a big ice cream sign.

words.def: to charm, sometimes in order to trick
words.ex: The singer’s lovely voice {beguiled} the whole audience.
words.ctx: The salesman’s friendly stories {beguiled} a young couple into buying a car they did not need; only later did they realize they had been tricked.
words.note: Beguile can be pure praise (a beguiling smile) or a warning (beguiled by a con man); read the context.

mn.cue: BE-GUILE: charm full of GUILE (sly tricks)
mn.text: Rex bows low and showers Nana Lou with flowers and compliments, and while she blushes, he slips her pie behind his back: he {beguiles} her.

scene.alt: A smooth-talking man bows with flowers to a blushing grandmother while her pie sneaks away behind him.

words.def: to tempt someone to go somewhere or do something
words.ex: Bright porch lights {lure} moths on summer nights.
words.ctx: The town hoped that a new park and lower rents would {lure} young families away from the crowded city and into its quiet streets.
words.etym: From Old French loire, a bundle of feathers swung on a cord to call a hunting falcon back.

mn.text: The shiny lure wiggles and sparkles in the water, and the curious fish swims closer and closer: the shine {lures} it in.

scene.alt: A shiny fishing lure sparkles in the water, and a curious fish swims toward it.

words.def: to force someone to act by using threats or pressure
words.ex: No one should be {coerced} into joining a club.
words.ctx: The pirate captain tried to {coerce} the townspeople into handing over their gold, threatening to block the harbor until they gave in.
words.etym: From Latin coercere, “to hold in, restrain”: co- (together) + arcere (to shut in).

mn.text: Captain Rex points his finger and roars, “Scrub the deck, or no supper!” He doesn’t ask; he {coerces} the crew.

scene.alt: On a ship, a pirate captain shouts a threat at a frightened boy scrubbing the deck.

words.def: to force or require someone to do something
words.ex: The heavy rain {compelled} us to cancel the game.
words.ctx: Though she wanted to keep reading, hunger finally {compelled} Maya to close her book and go downstairs for dinner.
words.etym: From Latin compellere, “to drive together”: com- (together) + pellere (to drive).
words.note: Compel can be neutral: the law compels drivers to stop at red lights.

mn.cue: com-PEL: the BELL pushes you up
mn.text: At six o’clock the alarm bell rings and rings, and Dev has no choice but to drag himself out of bed: the bell {compels} him.

scene.alt: A ringing alarm clock forces a sleepy teen to get out of bed.

words.def: to bully someone with stern words and looks
words.ex: The bossy captain tried to {browbeat} his crew into working through the night.
words.ctx: Rather than persuade the committee with facts, the chairman {browbeat} its members, glaring and shouting until they agreed just to make him stop.

mn.cue: a frowning BROW beats you DOWN
mn.text: Marcus lowers his bushy brows, glares and thunders until Sami gives up his turn at chess: Marcus {browbeats} him.

labels.text: a frowning BROW beats you DOWN

scene.alt: A big man glares and shouts at a nervous boy across a chess table.

words.def: to get money or something else by force or threats
words.ex: In the old tale, the pirates {extorted} gold from every ship that passed.
words.ctx: The scammer tried to {extort} money from the shop owner, threatening to post false reviews unless she paid him, but she called the police instead.
words.etym: From Latin extorquere, “to twist out”: ex- (out) + torquere (to twist).

mn.cue: EX-TORT: TWIST it OUT of you
mn.text: Rex blocks the little bridge and growls that no one may cross unless they hand over a coin: he {extorts} money from every traveler.

scene.alt: A sneaky man blocks a bridge and makes a sad boy hand over a coin to cross.

after.cap: From the softest touch to the hardest push.

after.html: beguile can praise (a beguiling melody) or warn (beguiled by a swindler), so read the sentence. coerce always means pressure or threats, while compel can be neutral: the law compels drivers to stop at red lights.

opts.s: With soft words and a bit of cheese, Zoe managed to {coax} the shy mouse out of its hole.

items.q: Which sentence uses compel in a neutral way, with no bullying?
choices: The rules compel every player to wear a helmet.
The bully compelled Pip to hand over his lunch.
The pirate compelled the sailors to give up their gold.
items.why: Compel simply means force or require. A rule can compel without any threat; the other two sentences describe coercion.

items.q: In “The music box’s tune beguiled the baby to sleep,” beguile means…
items.why: Here beguile is gentle: the tune charmed the baby. In other sentences it can mean to charm in order to trick.

items.q: True or false: to extort money is to earn it with hard work.
items.why: False. To extort is to get money by force or threats; the root tort means twist, as if twisting it out of someone.

items.q: Which word is the gentlest way to get someone to do something?
items.why: To coax is to persuade gently and patiently. The others use pressure, bullying or threats.
